reverseBrief.humanQuestion: Why does LAiDIES celebrate Hannah Fry, beyond her impressive title?
reverseBrief.promisedPayoff: A beginner reader learns what Fry actually contributes and leaves with three reusable questions to interrogate any automated decision that touches her life.
reverseBrief.distinctiveContribution: Making the mathematics inside automated decisions visible enough for ordinary people to question — recognized by the 2026 Leelavati Prize for increasing public awareness of mathematics.
reverseBrief.concreteExample: Hello World's opening dilemma: who should decide a criminal case — a person or an algorithm?
reverseBrief.readerConsequence: Trade-offs matter when a system shapes healthcare, justice or other consequential choices; neither human nor algorithm is automatically fairer.

transfer.scenario: A reader's employer introduces an automated CV-screening system that ranks job applicants before any human sees them. The reader has just read the Fry card and wants to know whether the card gives her anything usable here — a system the card never mentions.
transfer.question: Do the card's three closing questions transfer to this unseen system without requiring the reader to assert facts she cannot know?
transfer.answer: Yes. She can ask: What is this screening system trying to achieve — speed, cost, some definition of 'fit'? What might it miss — career gaps for caregiving, non-traditional experience, names it was not trained on? Who carries the consequence if it errs — the rejected applicant, not the vendor? Each is a question or possibility to investigate, not an asserted fact about the system's actual objective, inputs or effects.
transfer.assessment: The entry point transfers cleanly. The three questions are system-agnostic interrogatives, so applying them to a new consequential automated decision generates lines of inquiry rather than invented claims. The card's payoff survives outside its own example, which is the strongest evidence it is not decorative.

issues.finding: The opening sentence stacks an em-dash parenthetical inside a copular construction ('Fry's contribution—recognized by...—is making...'), the densest moment on the card. It remains parseable on first read and resolves immediately, so it is not material, but a lighter opening would serve absolute beginners slightly better.
issues.artifactExcerpt: Fry’s contribution—recognized by the 2026 Leelavati Prize for increasing public awareness of mathematics—is making the mathematics inside automated decisions visible enough for ordinary people to question.

learningDisposition.rationale: The candidate passes with only one minor stylistic observation. It exhibits none of the registered failure families (no glossary accumulation, award-list substitution, title-only biography, decorative analogy, generic action, or technical-explainer voice), and it correctly declines to inherit the Penguin promotional claim about algorithmic error rates. Nothing new warrants registry entry.

summary: PASS. The candidate About replaces a title-only incumbent with a real answer to 'why celebrate her': a sourced distinctive contribution (2026 Leelavati Prize grounding, Cambridge primary source), one concrete example (Hello World's human-versus-algorithm criminal-case dilemma, matching Penguin copy verbatim in substance), a reader consequence framed without inheriting publisher promotion ('not that one is automatically fairer'), and a genuinely transferable entry point (three questions that work on unseen automated systems such as CV screening). All locked fields — role, lesson, image, seven byte-identical links, freshness — are preserved per the change proof. All factual claims map to exact source passages; two are qualified as interpretation/synthesis within stated source limitations, none unsupported. The 100-word paragraph fits the shared card. One minor issue (dense opening em-dash construction) does not block. Incumbent negative control independently REJECTED as title-only biography lacking contribution, example, consequence and entry point.
